tips.title: Formulae are not given in the exam
tips.body: The specification says plainly that **formulae will not be provided** in Paper 1 or Paper 2. Gross profit, net profit, both margins and ARR all have to be memorised. Write them out from memory before you start revising the rest.

tips.title: Gross first, then net
tips.body: **Gross profit = revenue − cost of sales.** **Net profit = gross profit − other operating expenses and interest.** Net comes *from* gross, so work them in that order and you cannot take the same cost off twice.

tips.title: Both margins divide by revenue
tips.body: Gross margin and net margin **both divide by sales revenue**, never by cost or by each other. $(\text{profit} \div \text{revenue}) \times 100$. Dividing the net profit by the gross profit is the commonest wrong answer.

tips.title: For ARR, check what you have been given
tips.body: If the question gives **total profit**, divide it by the years straight away. If it gives **yearly returns**, you must **subtract the cost of the investment first** to turn returns into profit. Skipping that turned 15% into 40% in the example in this topic.

tips.title: A figure means nothing on its own
tips.body: A net margin of 15% is neither good nor bad until you compare it — with **last year**, with a **competitor**, or with the **target**. Every interpretation question is really asking "compared with what?".

steps.title: Gross profit and net profit
steps.body:
**Two profits, and the difference between them tells you where the money goes.**

**Gross profit** is what is left after paying for the goods themselves:

$$\text{Gross profit} = \text{sales revenue} - \text{cost of sales}$$

**Cost of sales** is what it cost to make or buy the things that were sold — the coffee beans, milk and cups for a café. It does **not** include rent or wages.

**Net profit** is what is left after everything else:

$$\text{Net profit} = \text{gross profit} - \text{other operating expenses and interest}$$

**Other operating expenses** are the running costs that are not the product itself: rent, wages, insurance, electricity, marketing. **Interest** on loans is included here too.

**Net profit is the one that matters** to an owner, because it is what is actually left. Gross profit is still useful, because it isolates whether the **product itself** makes money, separately from whether the **business around it** is affordable.

**The running example.** *Harbour Lights* is a small chain of coffee shops. Last year it had sales revenue of **£480,000**, cost of sales of **£192,000**, and other operating expenses and interest of **£216,000**.

steps.title: Profit margins
steps.body:
**A margin turns a profit into a percentage of revenue**, so businesses of different sizes can be compared.

$$\text{Gross profit margin (\%)} = \frac{\text{gross profit}}{\text{sales revenue}} \times 100$$

$$\text{Net profit margin (\%)} = \frac{\text{net profit}}{\text{sales revenue}} \times 100$$

**Both divide by sales revenue.** Neither divides by cost, and neither divides by the other. Dividing net profit by gross profit is the most common wrong answer in this topic.

**For Harbour Lights:** gross margin is $288,000 \div 480,000 \times 100 = $ **60%**, and net margin is $72,000 \div 480,000 \times 100 = $ **15%**.

**What each one tells you.** The **gross margin** shows how much of each pound of sales survives paying for the product. 60% is high, which is normal for coffee — the ingredients are cheap relative to the price.

The **net margin** shows how much survives everything. 15% means that of every £1 taken, **0.15** is profit and the rest has gone.

**The gap between them is the interesting part.** Here it is 45 percentage points, which is the rent, wages and other running costs. A business with a healthy gross margin and a thin net margin has a **good product and expensive overheads** — and that tells you where to look for savings.

**Net margin is always lower than gross margin**, because expenses can only ever be taken off, never added back. If yours comes out higher, you have made an arithmetic slip.

steps.title: What a margin is worth knowing
steps.body:
**A margin on its own means nothing.** 15% is neither good nor bad until it is compared with something. There are three comparisons worth making.

**Against previous years.** A net margin falling from 18% to 15% is a warning even though the business is still profitable. A margin rising is evidence that something is working.

**Against competitors.** Margins vary enormously by industry. A supermarket may run on 2–3% and be doing well; a software company may make 30% and be struggling. Comparing a café with a café is informative; comparing it with a car maker is not.

**Against the target.** If the business planned for 20% and achieved 15%, that gap is the story regardless of what anyone else achieved.

**Margin is not the same as total profit.** A business can have a high margin and low profit if it sells very little, or a low margin and high profit if it sells enormous volumes — which is exactly how supermarkets work. **Margin measures efficiency per pound of sales; profit measures how much money was actually made.** Questions often give you both, and they can point in different directions.

**How to improve each one.** The **gross margin** rises by raising the **price** or lowering the **cost of sales** — cheaper suppliers, less waste. The **net margin** rises through those, or by cutting **overheads**: renegotiating rent, using staff hours better. Knowing which margin is the problem tells you which lever to pull.

steps.title: Average rate of return
steps.body:
**ARR measures the return on a proposed investment**, as a percentage of what the investment cost — so two different projects can be compared.

$$\text{ARR (\%)} = \frac{\text{average annual profit}}{\text{cost of investment}} \times 100 \qquad \text{where average annual profit} = \frac{\text{total profit}}{\text{number of years}}$$

visuals.problem: Harbour Lights can buy a coffee machine for £50,000. It would produce a total profit of £90,000 over 3 years. Calculate the ARR.

steps.text: Check what you have been given: the question states **total profit** of £90,000 outright
steps.note: this is the common exam form — the profit is already net of the investment, so do not subtract anything
total profit divided by the number of years the business holds the asset

steps.text: Divide by the **cost of the investment**: £30,000 ÷ £50,000 = 0.6
steps.note: the cost of the investment, not the total profit — this is what the return is measured against
always give ARR as a percentage; a bare decimal loses the mark

steps.text: **The other form.** If a question gives **yearly returns** instead — £8,000 a year for 4 years on a £20,000 investment — first total them: £32,000
steps.note: returns are not yet profit, because the investment has not been paid for

steps.text: Then **subtract the cost** to get total profit: £32,000 − £20,000 = **£12,000**, giving ARR of **15%**
steps.note: skipping this gives 40%, nearly three times too high — read whether you were given returns or profit

steps.title: Using ARR to choose
steps.body:
**ARR exists to compare investments.** The specification suggests exactly this: work out the ARR of extending a factory and the ARR of buying new machinery, and judge which the business should choose.

**A higher ARR is better**, all else being equal, because more profit is earned per pound invested. If the coffee machine returns 60% and a refurbishment returns 15%, the machine looks the stronger investment.

**But ARR should never decide it alone**, and saying so is where the evaluation marks are.

**What ARR ignores:**

- **The size of the investment.** A 60% return on £50,000 and a 60% return on £5,000 are the same percentage and very different amounts of money.
- **Whether the business can afford it.** A high ARR is no use if paying for it leaves the business unable to meet its bills.
- **When the money arrives.** ARR treats a profit in year 3 as worth the same as one in year 1, and a business short of cash cares a great deal about the difference.
- **Risk.** The figures are **forecasts**. A project with a lower ARR but far more certain returns may be the better decision.
- **Everything non-financial** — staff, customers, reputation, and whether the project fits what the business is trying to be.

**So the shape of a good answer is:** calculate it, say what it means, then say what it leaves out.

steps.title: Using quantitative data
steps.body:
**The specification asks you to use and interpret quantitative business data to support, inform and justify business decisions**, from four kinds of source.

**Information from graphs and charts.** Read the **axes** and the **units** before the shape. A line rising steeply may be rising by very little if the axis starts at 90 rather than 0 — a genuinely common way of being misled.

**Financial data.** Profit and loss figures, margins, ARR, cash flow. These say whether the business is making money and where it is going.

**Marketing data.** Market research: what customers say they want, which products sell, how promotions performed.

**Market data.** Market share, changes in costs, changes in prices — information about the **market**, not just this business. Falling sales matter very differently if the whole market is shrinking than if rivals are growing.

**How to use data in an answer.** **Quote the figure**, say what it **shows**, then say what the business should **do** about it. *Sales fell 12%* is data. *Sales fell 12% while the market grew 3%, so Harbour Lights is losing share to competitors and should look at why customers are switching* is an answer.

**Always look for a comparison in the data you are given.** Exam extracts almost always include something to compare against, and the comparison is usually the point of the question.

steps.title: The limits of financial information
steps.body:
**The specification asks for the use and limitations of financial information**, and the limitations carry most of the marks.

**It is historic.** Accounts describe what **has** happened. They are evidence about the future only to the extent that next year resembles last year, which is exactly what cannot be assumed when something has changed.

**It does not explain why.** A figure shows that the net margin fell from 18% to 15%. It does not say whether that was a rent rise, a supplier price increase, discounting to hold customers, or a one-off repair. The number raises the question; it does not answer it.

**It ignores qualitative factors** entirely. Staff morale, customer loyalty, the strength of the brand, the quality of management, what competitors are about to do — none of it appears, and all of it affects what happens next.

**It can be presented favourably.** A business chooses which figures to emphasise and over what period. A "record year" may look different measured over three.

**It needs context to mean anything.** One figure is not information. Compared with **last year**, a **competitor**, or the **target**, it becomes evidence.

**So financial information is necessary but not sufficient.** The strongest answers say exactly that: use the figures, and then say what else you would want to know before deciding. For Harbour Lights, a 15% net margin is a starting point — whether it is good depends on last year, on other cafés, and on why it is where it is.

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
*Harbour Lights* had sales revenue of **£480,000**, cost of sales of **£192,000**, and other operating expenses and interest of **£216,000**.

**Part A.**

1. Write the formula for gross profit.
2. Write the formula for net profit margin.
3. Write the formula for ARR.

**Part B.**

4. Calculate Harbour Lights' gross profit and gross profit margin.
5. Calculate its net profit and net profit margin.
6. A machine costs £50,000 and gives a total profit of £90,000 over 3 years. Calculate the ARR.

**Part C.**

7. A refurbishment costs £20,000 and returns £8,000 a year for 4 years. Calculate its ARR — read the question carefully.
8. Explain two limitations of using ARR to choose between the two projects.
9. Harbour Lights' net margin has fallen from 18% to 15%. Explain what else you would need to know before advising it.

Question 7 gives **returns**, not profit. Question 6 gives **profit**. Treat them differently.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Learn the formulae — they are not provided.** The specification states it explicitly for both papers. Gross profit, net profit, both margins and ARR.

**Both margins divide by revenue.** Never by cost, never by each other. Dividing net profit by gross profit is the single most common error here, and it produces a plausible-looking percentage, so it is rarely noticed.

**Check net against gross.** Net margin must be **lower** than gross margin, because expenses can only be subtracted. If it comes out higher, there is an arithmetic slip to find.

**For ARR, read what you were given.** **Total profit** → divide by years immediately. **Yearly returns** → total them and **subtract the cost of the investment first**. In this topic that is the difference between **15%** and **40%**, and the wrong figure would change the recommendation completely.

**Explain the gap between the margins.** A high gross margin with a thin net margin means a **good product carried by expensive overheads**, and that points at rent and wages rather than at suppliers. That single observation does the work of a paragraph.

**Distinguish margin from total profit.** High margin with low sales is a small profit; low margin with enormous sales is a large one. Questions often give both, and they can point in opposite directions.

**Always compare.** A figure alone is not evidence. Against **last year**, a **competitor**, or the **target** — and against the **market**, since sales falling 12% while the market grows 3% is a different problem from sales falling in a shrinking market.

**Give the limitations properly.** Financial information is **historic**, does **not explain why**, ignores **qualitative factors**, and can be **presented favourably**. The strongest sentence you can write is that the figures are **necessary but not sufficient** — then say what else you would want to know.

**On ARR specifically, name what it ignores**: the **size** of the sum, the **timing** of the returns, the **risk** in a forecast, and **affordability**. A project with a lower ARR and far more certain returns can be the better decision.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Gross profit = sales revenue − cost of sales.**
- **Net profit = gross profit − other operating expenses and interest.**
- **Gross profit margin (%) = (gross profit ÷ sales revenue) × 100.**
- **Net profit margin (%) = (net profit ÷ sales revenue) × 100.**
- **Both margins divide by revenue**, never by each other.
- Net margin is **always lower** than gross margin.
- Harbour Lights: gross **£288,000** (60%), net **£72,000** (15%).
- The **gap** between the margins is the overheads.
- **ARR (%) = (average annual profit ÷ cost of investment) × 100.**
- **Average annual profit = total profit ÷ number of years.**
- Given **returns** rather than profit, **subtract the investment cost first**.
- **Formulae are not provided in the exam.**
- **Margin is not total profit** — high margin with low sales is a small profit.
- A figure means nothing without a **comparison**: last year, a rival, or the target.
- Financial information is **historic**, does not say **why**, and ignores **qualitative** factors.

questions.prompt: Harbour Lights, a small chain of coffee shops, had sales revenue of £480,000, cost of sales of £192,000, and other operating expenses and interest of £216,000. Its net profit margin has fallen from 18% last year to its current level. Analyse Harbour Lights' financial performance.
questions.solution:
Taking the figures in order, **gross profit** is sales revenue minus cost of sales: $£480\,000 - £192\,000 = \textbf{£288\,000}$. The **gross profit margin** is therefore $(288\,000 \div 480\,000) \times 100 = \textbf{60\%}$.

**Net profit** is gross profit minus other operating expenses and interest: $£288\,000 - £216\,000 = \textbf{£72\,000}$, giving a **net profit margin** of $(72\,000 \div 480\,000) \times 100 = \textbf{15\%}$.

**The gross margin of 60% is strong**, and it is what you would expect of a coffee shop: beans, milk and cups cost very little against the price of a drink. It tells us the **product itself is profitable** and that Harbour Lights is neither underpricing nor being badly treated by its suppliers.

**The 45 percentage point gap** between the two margins is the more revealing figure. That gap is £216,000 of **rent, wages, electricity and loan interest** — overheads consuming three-quarters of the gross profit. Coffee shops sit on expensive high-street sites and are labour-intensive, so this is not surprising, but it does mean the business's profitability is decided far more by its **overheads** than by its pricing or its suppliers.

**The fall from 18% to 15%** is what should concern the owners. The business is still profitable, so there is no crisis, but a three percentage point fall on £480,000 of revenue is about **£14,400** of lost profit — a fifth of what remains. If the trend continues at that rate, the margin would be near zero within five years.

The chain matters here. A falling net margin with a **healthy gross margin** implies the problem is in **overheads rather than in the product**: rent may have been reviewed upwards, wages increased, or energy costs risen. Each of those flows straight from operating expenses into net profit without touching the 60% gross margin at all — which is precisely the pattern the figures show.

**Judgement.** Harbour Lights is a **fundamentally sound business with a cost problem rather than a product problem**. The 60% gross margin is the evidence for that, and it is the reason to be optimistic: a business whose product did not make money would be in a far worse position.

But the figures alone cannot say what to do, because they show **that** the margin fell and not **why**. Before acting I would want to know which expenses rose and whether the rise is permanent — a rent review is a lasting change requiring a structural response, while a one-off repair is not. I would also want last year's **gross** margin: if that has held at 60% the diagnosis above is confirmed, whereas if it too has slipped then the problem is broader than overheads.

**The fall from 18% to 15%** is what should concern the owners. The business is still profitable, so there is no crisis, but a three percentage point fall on £480,000 of revenue is about **£14,400** of lost profit — a fifth of what remains. If the trend continues at that rate, the margin would be near zero within five years.

The chain matters here. A falling net margin with a **healthy gross margin** implies the problem is in **overheads rather than in the product**: rent may have been reviewed upwards, wages increased, or energy costs risen. Each of those flows straight from operating expenses into net profit without touching the 60% gross margin at all — which is precisely the pattern the figures show.

**Judgement.** Harbour Lights is a **fundamentally sound business with a cost problem rather than a product problem**. The 60% gross margin is the evidence for that, and it is the reason to be optimistic: a business whose product did not make money would be in a far worse position.

But the figures alone cannot say what to do, because they show **that** the margin fell and not **why**. Before acting I would want to know which expenses rose and whether the rise is permanent — a rent review is a lasting change requiring a structural response, while a one-off repair is not. I would also want last year's **gross** margin: if that has held at 60% the diagnosis above is confirmed, whereas if it too has slipped then the problem is broader than overheads.

questions.prompt: Harbour Lights is choosing between two investments. Project A is a coffee machine costing £50,000 with a total profit of £90,000 over 3 years. Project B is a refurbishment costing £20,000 returning £8,000 a year for 4 years. Its net profit last year was £72,000. Evaluate which project Harbour Lights should choose.
questions.solution:
**Project A** gives its **total profit** directly: £90,000 over 3 years. Average annual profit is $£90\,000 \div 3 = £30\,000$, so the ARR is $(30\,000 \div 50\,000) \times 100 = \textbf{60\%}$.

**Project B** gives **yearly returns**, which is a different thing. Total returns are $£8000 \times 4 = £32\,000$, but returns are not profit until the investment has been recovered, so total profit is $£32\,000 - £20\,000 = £12\,000$. Average annual profit is $£12\,000 \div 4 = £3000$, giving an ARR of $(3000 \div 20\,000) \times 100 = \textbf{15\%}$.

It is worth noting that failing to subtract the £20,000 would give 40% for Project B and make the comparison look much closer than it is — reading which form the figures come in is essential here.

**On the financial evidence, Project A is far stronger.** A 60% ARR against 15% means each pound invested earns four times as much per year. In cash terms A returns £30,000 a year against B's £3,000, so A is better both as a rate and in absolute amount — which is not always the case, and settles a great deal here.

**But ARR alone should not decide it**, and several things weigh the other way.

**Affordability and risk.** £50,000 is a large commitment against a net profit of **£72,000** — it would absorb roughly **seven months of the entire year's profit**. If it requires a loan, the interest adds to operating expenses permanently, and those expenses are exactly where the business's margin has already been under pressure. Project B at £20,000 is a far lighter commitment that could likely be funded from retained profit without borrowing at all.

**The forecasts are forecasts.** A machine's output can be estimated fairly reliably; the returns from a refurbishment depend on customers choosing to visit more often, which is a softer prediction. That argues **for** A on risk grounds, though both figures should be treated with caution.

**Timing.** ARR treats every year alike. A returns over 3 years and B over 4, so A recovers its money sooner — which matters to a business whose margin is falling and whose cash position is therefore tightening.

**Non-financial factors** favour B, and they are not trivial. A refurbishment affects what **every** customer sees on every visit, supporting the premium a coffee shop charges for somewhere pleasant to sit. A machine improves what is served but not the experience around it. A tired-looking café can lose customers however good the coffee, and that damage would not show in either ARR calculation.

**Conclusion.** Harbour Lights should choose **Project A**, but the decision depends on **how it is financed**. The financial case is not close — 60% against 15%, and four times the annual return — and a business with a falling net margin needs the stronger return.

The qualification matters, though. If £50,000 can only be raised by borrowing on terms that add materially to the operating expenses already squeezing the margin, the business would be treating a margin problem by making its overheads worse. In that case the sensible route is **B first**, funded from retained profit, with A revisited once the cash position is stronger.

What I would want before committing is the **breakdown of the rise in operating expenses** behind the fall from 18% to 15%. If overheads are still rising, neither project addresses the actual problem, and spending £50,000 would be solving the wrong thing.

examTechnique.body:
**Memorise the formulae — they are not provided.** Work **gross first, then net**, and remember **both margins divide by revenue**. Check that net margin is **lower** than gross margin.

For **ARR**, read whether you were given **total profit** or **yearly returns**; returns need the investment **subtracted first**. Then interpret: compare with last year, a rival or the target.
examinerErrors: Dividing net profit by gross profit instead of by revenue.
Giving a net margin higher than the gross margin.
Forgetting to subtract the investment cost when given yearly returns.
Leaving ARR as a decimal instead of a percentage.
Including rent or wages in cost of sales.
Treating a margin as though it were the total profit.
Quoting a figure without comparing it to anything.
Giving "the figures could be wrong" as the limitation of financial information.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer writes the formulae from memory, works **gross then net**, and checks that the net margin came out **lower**. On ARR it notices **which form** the question used and subtracts the investment when given returns. It reads the **gap** between the margins as overheads, and separates **margin** from **total profit**. Every figure is **compared** — with last year, a competitor, the target or the market — and when it evaluates an investment it names what ARR **ignores**: size, timing, risk and affordability. It closes by saying what it would still need to know, because the figures show **that** something changed and never **why**.
